item.title: OpenClaw at one: its chief architect on a year of explosive growth, wooing the enterprise, and being Meta’s muse
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
It’s been a whirlwind 12 months for OpenClaw, the open source personal AI agent used for everything from managing calendars

The post OpenClaw at one: its chief architect on a year of explosive growth, wooing the enterprise, and being Meta’s muse appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
It’s been a whirlwind 12 months for OpenClaw, the open source personal AI agent used for everything from managing calendars and email to booking flights and restaurants.

On Nov. 24, 2025 — exactly a year ago today — Austrian software developer Peter Steinberger made the first commit for Warelay, a small WhatsApp relay designed to let users trigger actions on their computer through WhatsApp. It briefly became Clawd, a play on Claude and its lobster mascot, before Anthropic’s legal team “politely” asked Steinberger to reconsider the name. After another short-lived stint as Moltbot, the project finally settled on OpenClaw at the end of January, 2026.

OpenClaw has become one of the most closely watched open source projects in AI. That excitement ultimately led OpenAI to hire Steinberger in February, with the project eventually moving into an independent foundation backed by companies including OpenAI itself, GitHub, and Nvidia.

Meanwhile, the Foundation has also stepped up its enterprise push, while the arrival of OpenClaw 2.0 focused heavily on making the project easier to install and use.

Ahead of the one-year anniversary, The New Stack caught up with Vincent Koc to chat all things OpenClaw, including how the project has matured, its growing enterprise ambitions, and how it has influenced projects from some of the biggest names in technology.

OpenClaw grows up… and becomes Meta’s muse

As an open source project available under an MIT license, anyone is able to take OpenClaw and do more or less as they please with it — including building their own products and services around it. However, its influence also extends into the broader agentic AI realm, as evidenced in September when Meta launched Muse, described as the “world’s first personal AI agent built for everyone.”

Like OpenClaw, Muse is designed to act on a user’s behalf across apps, retain personal context, and carry out tasks through a browser. But when Muse hit the market in September, Ansh Nanda, co-founder and CEO of Vibecode, noted that the similarities went considerably further, calling it “LITERALLY Openclaw for normies,” adding that “it’s actually just openclaw.”

To support that assertion, Nanda shared a screenshot in which Muse compared its own system files with the OpenClaw GitHub repository. It reported the same set of workspace file names — including SOUL.md, MEMORY.md, USER.md, IDENTITY.md, TOOLS.md, HEARTBEAT.md, AGENTS.md and BOOTSTRAP.md — and said parts of its SOUL.md closely matched OpenClaw’s.

Nat Friedman, ex-GitHub CEO who’s now heading up Meta’s AI products and applied research unit, didn’t shy away from the influence. He said the company had developed Muse “from scratch,” but added: “…it is definitely heavily inspired as a product by openclaw.”

Indeed, Friedman said that Meta’s goal was to make an OpenClaw-like experience secure and easy enough for a much broader audience. When pressed on why Muse was sailing so close to the exact file names, Friedman replied: “We thought that Peter [Steinberger] got those things exactly right!”

Meta, of course, wasn’t the only company influenced by OpenClaw. And in some respects, the intense hype that surrounded the project earlier in the year has moved elsewhere as a growing number of companies have launched agents of their own.

“From our perspective, I think it’s nice that the hype has died down, the spotlight’s off of us, and we can get focused on actually building a good product without everyone having ‘lobster fever’.”

“There’s always going to be hype in the zeitgeist, and there’s going to be the new shiny object that everyone gravitates towards,” Koc tells The New Stack. “From our perspective, I think it’s nice that the hype has died down, the spotlight’s off of us, and we can get focused on actually building a good product without everyone having ‘lobster fever’.”

Getting hooked on OpenClaw

Koc himself first encountered OpenClaw before most of that attention arrived. At the time, he was working at AI evaluation and observability company Comet, and started to notice the project cropping up repeatedly online around the tail end of 2025.

He installed it out of curiosity and, despite encountering plenty of bugs, spent the next four or five days using it almost continuously. What caught his attention was the way it could change its own code in response to instructions, but also how different the interaction felt compared with the AI chatbots he had been using.

“It was like you’re talking to a mate on WhatsApp or iMessage. It felt very personal.”

“There was ChatGPT and Claude, but they felt somewhat robotic — it felt like I was still talking to an agent,” Koc explains. “Whereas with this [OpenClaw], it was just this continual chat thread, it was like you’re talking to a mate on WhatsApp or iMessage. It felt very personal.”

Koc soon began contributing himself, initially concentrating on security vulnerabilities as a way of getting Steinberger’s attention. That led to him becoming a security maintainer, before his remit expanded into the project’s wider architecture. By the time the pair discussed Koc working on OpenClaw full time, he says he had become its second-largest code contributor.

The project’s future became a more pressing question in February, however, when OpenAI hired Steinberger. “Yes, I could totally see how OpenClaw could become a huge company,” he wrote at the time. “And no, it’s not really exciting for me. I’m a builder at heart.”

Instead, Steinberger said the project would remain open and independent under a foundation, with OpenAI sponsoring it and enabling him to continue working on it. That foundation was formally established in July, bringing in its first full-time team, including Koc as chief architect. Steinberger remains heavily involved in the project’s engineering direction, Koc says, even as a larger team has assumed responsibility for the Foundation’s day-to-day work.

“He was the founder of this project, he was there from day one,” Koc says. “His vision and his involvement matters deeply, but beyond that, we have a large team that’s looking at everything from our corporate relationships to marketing and events.”

And the list of companies now involved extends well beyond OpenAI. Alongside sponsors including GitHub and Nvidia, OpenClaw has maintainers from Microsoft, Tencent, Atlassian and others. And Koc says the Foundation is working with labs, as well as technology companies across Asia and Europe.

Koc says those companies have different motivations for getting involved, but OpenClaw’s independence is ultimately a big part of the attraction.

“Different companies have joined for different reasons,” Koc says. “I think individuals in these companies saw the potential, saw we are independent, we are open source, but also we’re not venture backed. So it creates this really interesting thing, where they can see us like another Linux or Mozilla — something that’s going to live longer.”

“It creates this really interesting thing, where they can see us like another Linux or Mozilla — something that’s going to live longer.”

Microsoft offers one of the clearest example of where that involvement can lead. In June, it unveiled Scout, an always-on personal agent for Microsoft 365 powered by OpenClaw. Microsoft corporate vice president Omar Shahine said at the time that the company had added the identity, credential, access and security controls needed to make it suitable for enterprise use.

Microsoft also contributed policy-conformance work directly upstream to OpenClaw, allowing organizations to check deployments against their security and compliance requirements and produce an audit-ready result.

Nvidia has taken a similar route with NemoClaw, which builds on OpenClaw while adding its own security, privacy and policy controls through the company’s OpenShell runtime.

Scout was renamed Autopilot in September as part of Microsoft’s revamped Copilot lineup, but the OpenClaw connection remains. And with both Microsoft and Nvidia building products around OpenClaw, the Foundation itself has also turned its attention to making the project more suitable for large organizations.

Claw courts the enterprise

The growing corporate involvement comes as OpenClaw itself makes a concerted push into the enterprise. In September, the Foundation launched OpenClaw Enterprise, an open source, self-hostable, vendor-neutral platform designed to give companies a central way to deploy, govern and isolate persistent agents.

The project remains “pre-1.0,” and is currently intended for internal pilots, but its remit is clear: give IT teams control over who can deploy agents, what those agents can access, and how their activity is audited. The OpenClaw Control Plane adds multi-tenancy, permissions and security boundaries while letting companies choose their own models, harnesses and infrastructure.

Part of that work has also involved reducing what gets installed by default. OpenClaw moved integrations including Slack, WhatsApp, Matrix and Amazon Bedrock out of its core dependency path, meaning their dependencies only arrive when those capabilities are actually installed.

“We’ve carved out the code into plugins,” Koc says. “If you’re not using something, it doesn’t get installed.”

The Foundation has also worked with technology companies on scanning and auditing OpenClaw skills. In June, Koc and researchers from OpenClaw and Nvidia published a study covering tens of thousands of public skill versions, comparing results from VirusTotal, OpenClaw’s own static analysis and Nvidia’s SkillSpector.

The three approaches frequently identified different risks. Just 0.69% of skills were flagged by all three, while 81.9% of those flagged were picked up by only one. OpenClaw subsequently combined those signals through ClawScan, alongside provenance, metadata and moderation history, and released the underlying dataset for outside researchers.

“There’s not one way to make everything absolutely safe and secure,” Koc said. “Security is going to be this evolving thing — there’s no one-size-fits-all.”

Koc also says that this kind of work is beginning to change the conversation with large organizations. He compared the initial response to OpenClaw with the early corporate reaction to ChatGPT and Claude, when security concerns prompted some companies to pull the plug.

“Everyone in enterprise were like, ‘shut it down. This is dangerous,’” Koc says. “I feel like there’s an element of that here now.”

But, he suggests, that response is easing as companies better understand how OpenClaw works and the security risks involved. He also says that it is being used by Fortune 100 companies, other large enterprises and governments, including across teams and projects and, in some cases, with individual employees running their own instances.

Larger deployments also raise a new set of questions. If employees eventually have separate personal and work agents, for example, OpenClaw will have to determine how those agents communicate, what information they can share, and how they coordinate things such as calendars without crossing organizational boundaries.

“What I personally don’t want to see is this world where we have all these different agents and none of them can collaborate or work together.”

More broadly, Koc is thinking about what happens as more companies build agents of their own.

“What I personally don’t want to see is this world where we have all these different agents and none of them can collaborate or work together, and it becomes like you have to buy into some ecosystem to make things work,” Koc says.

What’s next for OpenClaw

Released at the end of August, much of OpenClaw 2.0 was ultimately about removing friction. The release began as an effort to simplify installation and rebuild the browser experience, before expanding into a much broader overhaul spanning memory, skills, native apps, plugins, security and other parts of the project.

That push has continued since. OpenClaw has introduced simpler native installers and onboarding, with Koc saying the goal is eventually to get as close as possible to a click-and-go experience — install OpenClaw, configure it, set up a local model where appropriate, and have it ready to use without requiring people to spend time configuring servers or dependencies.

Koc himself is also willing to push OpenClaw further in his own life than many users might be comfortable with. In some instances, he gives it access to his email, phone, computer and other personal data, acknowledging that doing so carries some risk but arguing that he needs to experience this himself if he is helping build the product.

“I know there’s some risk attached to that, but I feel like if I’m working on the edge and creating a product like this, I need to embrace the unknown a little bit more than everyone else,” Koc says. “There needs to be an element of me dogfooding this and understanding how it works.”

All of this raises an obvious question, particularly given the comparison with Meta’s personal AI agent: does this all ultimately lead to OpenClaw ultimately becoming the same kind of polished consumer product?

“Probably not in the vein of Muse, but we are looking at how we simplify the experience as much as possible,” Koc says. “As much as an open source project can, one that doesn’t want to handle infrastructure, and still let you run it the way you want to run it.”

So while there are clear similarities between OpenClaw and products such as Muse, they are ultimately different propositions. Meta can manage the underlying infrastructure and hide much of the complexity from the user; OpenClaw is trying to make things easier while preserving the ability to choose where it runs, which models it uses and how much control the user retains.

Beyond ease of use, multiplayer is also emerging as another significant part of what comes next. OpenClaw Multiplayer lets multiple people work with and steer the same agent while retaining the same context, an idea that grew out of the Foundation’s own experiments with shared agent sessions. It says around 50 people at the Foundation are already using the same shared environment.

“We’re trying to reinvent how we work as a team and improve the way we work with agents, and then whatever that ends up becoming is what we end up shipping to the community,” Koc says.

As for what OpenClaw 3.0 might look like, Koc says the team is still working that out. But the same principle appears likely to shape it: its direction, he suggests, will be determined largely by the problems OpenClaw’s own developers encounter while using the project.

“Whatever’s slowing us down, whatever’s making it harder for us to build OpenClaw, that is what we’re going to solve next, and we’re going to give that back to the community,” Koc says.

The post OpenClaw at one: its chief architect on a year of explosive growth, wooing the enterprise, and being Meta’s muse appeared first on The New Stack.

Vincent Koc spotted OpenClaw’s potential early, joining Peter Steinberger as a core maintainer. Now the Foundation’s chief architect, he’s helping turn a scrappy side project into one of the biggest open source bets in agentic AI.

item.title: Vercel will make AI providers prove they don’t keep prompts. Here’s why it matters for developers.
item.dc:creator: Luke James
item.description:
Since April, developers using Vercel’s AI Gateway have been able to request provider-level zero data retention (ZDR). Vercel says its

The post Vercel will make AI providers prove they don’t keep prompts. Here’s why it matters for developers. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Since April, developers using Vercel’s AI Gateway have been able to request provider-level zero data retention (ZDR). Vercel says its existing provider-level ZDR routing relies on providers’ policies and agreements with the company; the new tier adds a requirement for published independent audits. 

On Monday, Vercel announced Audited ZDR, a tier that will admit providers only after independent security firms test their retention claims against their code, infrastructure, and live traffic and publish the reports. Vercel says a planned team-wide toggle will restrict routing and failover to providers with qualifying published audits. The announcement does not give a separate general-availability date for the toggle.

Vercel says launch partners Baseten, Modal, and Wafer have begun their audits, with reports expected by December 8. Each provider will enter the tier once its qualifying report is published. 

The announcement follows research published November 19 by industrial cybersecurity firm Dragos, which sent about 2 million prompts containing trackable credentials and URLs to AI services. Vercel’s announcement does not cite that research. On Sunday, OpenRouter said it’d removed three providers and stripped 125 endpoints of their ZDR eligibility as a result.

Singing like a canary

Dragos’s prompts carried canary tokens: AWS keys (real ones, tied to empty, fully logged accounts) and unique links that alert whoever planted them when they’re subsequently used. The company says that data from “at least three AI providers was exposed,” and none of the three knew until Dragos told them. 

The company says that data from ‘at least three AI providers was exposed,’ and none of the three knew until Dragos told them.

Dragos also reported cases in which privacy settings appeared not to be honored.

According to Chief Research Officer HD Moore, an unnamed Chinese AI lab’s systems fetched unique URLs from more than half the prompts sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of requests marked for no data collection or ZDR. Moore attributes such failures to deliberate practices or processing bugs; those findings do not establish that every provider ignores ZDR settings.

Routers can add further intermediaries between an application and the provider running a model, complicating the task of tracing where prompts go. “Some routers are open marketplaces where the seller with the lowest price gets the request,” Moore writes, and a privacy flag “only binds the first hop.” 

Vercel has also offered free stealth models, including Cat Jam, but its announcement explicitly said ZDR was unavailable and prompts could be retained for safety reasons.

OpenRouter, which Stripe agreed to buy in August, published a notice Sunday. It says it off-boarded three providers, pulled 125 endpoints from ZDR eligibility (some purely as a precaution), and notified affected customers. The notice does not identify the three off-boarded providers. It separately links to statements from Atlas Cloud, Novita, Phala, and Together, without identifying them as the three removed providers.

OpenRouter says the findings did not show a breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter itself. The providers’ statements describe different issues: Atlas Cloud and Novita discuss upstream MiniMax request handling, while Phala and Together describe security incidents. 

It’s also planning to run its own Dragos-style canary tests, “adapting the researchers’ testing approach so we can run these checks on an ongoing basis,” and will require validation before any endpoint gets ZDR status back. 

Receipts, not promises

In its Audited ZDR announcement, Vercel says contracts and self-attestation aren’t enough for proprietary code or regulated data. It asks, among other things, whether prompts end up in debug logs or crash dumps, and whether support tools can find them. Vercel presents Audited ZDR as the next step after April’s team-wide ZDR and its own ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification. 

Vercel says contracts and self-attestation aren’t enough for proprietary code or regulated data.

An audit would cover everything from request logs, traces, and crash dumps to prompt caches and support tools. The audit would also cover any training, fine-tuning, or eval datasets. To qualify for the audited tier, a provider must also demonstrate that ZDR requests do not fail over to non-ZDR endpoints, tools, or features. 

Auditors review the provider’s serving-path source code and infrastructure configuration, then send marked prompts through the gateway and search logging, caching, and storage systems for traces. Published reports must disclose exceptions and fix status, with redactions limited to exploit detail.

Vercel is also running its own canaries. The gateway creates unique URLs connected to a model, slips them into ZDR-flagged prompts, and logs any request that comes back. 

“Any request to a canary URL triggers an investigation into the provider and model involved,” a Vercel spokesperson tells The New Stack.

“Any request to a canary URL triggers an investigation into the provider and model involved,” a Vercel spokesperson tells The New Stack, though “a URL fetch does not by itself establish that a provider retained data.” 

The canaries have limits, and Vercel says so: they can’t detect prompts written to disk and never read. Independent audits examine a provider’s systems at a point in time; canaries add monitoring between audits. Neither should be presented as an unconditional guarantee against future breaches.

Where your prompts end up

Teams can already use ZDR either per request (zeroDataRetention: true in providerOptions.gateway) or through the team-wide setting, which costs $0.10 per 1,000 requests. Both require a Pro or Enterprise plan or purchased AI Gateway credits. The planned Audited ZDR tier would further restrict routing to providers with qualifying published audits. Its announcement does not specify a separate surcharge.

Existing ZDR also has scope limits: provider-run tools and short-lived prompt caches can be treated differently under provider policies, so teams should check what their chosen route covers. 

With open-weight models, the inference host may be a different company from the model developer, so teams need to check who actually processes their requests; open-weight models handled 56% of tokens on Vercel’s gateway in August. 

Coding agents add another potential exposure: their requests can include credentials and other sensitive material available in their context. Dragos recommends choosing upstream providers explicitly rather than accepting a router’s default pool. 

Dragos also recommends planting canaries as an additional detection measure. Separately, Vercel’s gateway offers routing controls: teams can filter routing by the country where a provider’s parent company is headquartered, or pin inference to the US, Europe, Australia, or Japan. Provider headquarters and inference location are separate controls. 

Vercel’s announcement does not name the firms auditing the three launch partners, though each report is to be published under its auditor’s name. Each provider “engages an independent security firm to run the audit,” the spokesperson said. 

“The firm then tests the provider’s zero data retention policy across the serving path for every model, endpoint, feature, and tool that handles AI Gateway traffic.” The announcement does not specify when other existing ZDR providers might join the audited tier. Providers engage the independent firms; Vercel is not describing audits conducted by its own staff. 

Vercel says it expects the launch partners’ audit reports by December 8. That is an expected report-publication date, rather than a confirmed general-availability date for the entire tier. 

The post Vercel will make AI providers prove they don’t keep prompts. Here’s why it matters for developers. appeared first on The New Stack.
Canary tests show privacy flags don't always stick. Vercel now wants published audits as proof, and Baseten, Modal, and Wafer are up first.

item.title: Anthropic’s Claude Ship lets Claude approve routine pull requests
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Anthropic on Monday launched Claude Ship, a set of three agents that can review pull requests (PRs), fix them, and approve

The post Anthropic’s Claude Ship lets Claude approve routine pull requests appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic on Monday launched Claude Ship, a set of three agents that can review pull requests (PRs), fix them, and approve them — if the team’s policy allows.

The first of these three agents, Code Review, already became generally available in October. The other two are new and in beta.

PR Steward pushes fixes for failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and review feedback, while Claude Approvals reads a policy in the team’s GitHub repository to determine whether a PR still needs a human reviewer.

For a while now, Anthropic has been saying that Claude already writes most of the code for Claude Code. The slow part, the company argues, now comes after a developer opens a PR. By the time the review comes back, that developer may have already moved on to something else. This means even a minor change means putting that work aside to push a fix, wait for the checks to run again, and track down someone to approve it.

Most companies don’t work at the pace of Anthropic, but the bottleneck of code reviews — and the DevOps lifecycle in general — is something that slows down virtually all businesses at this point.

Who has to sign off?

Most companies won’t be willing to completely trust AI to review all code, but as Anthropic notes, maybe it means not every change needs two reviewers to agree, for example.

In practice, this could mean a change to a mission-critical billing service would still need two reviewers besides the author, including someone from the payments team. But for most other code, a clean review from Claude could cut the number of necessary human approvals to just one. And, if the change only touches documentation, that same review lets Claude approve it on its own.

To set all of this up, teams write those rules in .claude/approvals.yml, where they can also define their own classifiers in natural language. Anthropic recommends running the policy in observe-only mode first to see which PRs Claude would approve, before making its sign-off a required check.

PR Steward does its work before a PR gets to that point. It can act on feedback from people and other review tools, but it can’t approve or merge a PR. After each push, it comments on what it changed and how to undo it.

Admins can enable Claude Ship for a whole repository, and developers can also run /ship in Claude Code to push a change, open a PR, and work through feedback and failing checks. The command runs locally for up to seven days, so the session has to stay open and the computer awake.

How GitHub, Cursor, and CodeRabbit handle approvals

Unsurprisingly, other coding tool vendors are tackling the same bottleneck. GitHub, for example, introduced approvals for Copilot code review on Sept. 1 and made them generally available on Oct. 28. Admins can restrict which paths Copilot can approve.

Cursor’s PR Routing & Approval agent applies a team’s risk threshold and reads the APPROVAL_POLICY.md file closest to the changed file. CodeRabbit lets teams set separate limits for merge risk and security risk in .coderabbit.yaml.

GitHub’s Max review level, now in public preview, also uses models from different providers and reconciles their findings. In Claude Ship, all three agents use Claude.

How Anthropic uses Claude Ship

Anthropic says the Claude Code team uses Claude Ship on many of its own PRs. When a customer flagged a misleading passage in the Analytics API docs, for example, a product manager asked Claude

Tag, the company’s Slack agent, about it. Tag opened a PR, Code Review found nothing blocking it, and a docs reviewer signed off. The fix merged that evening.

From June to September, the company says, the team more than doubled the number of PRs it merged while the share it reverted fell by more than 40 percent.

It’s worth noting, though, that Claude Ship covers only part of that overall process. The team’s own engineering post from October, for example, also describes a separate security review that can block a merge.

TELUS Digital and Carvana are among the early customers. In a statement Anthropic provided, Vatsal Bhatt, director of engineering at TELUS Digital, says, “We keep a human in the loop.” He adds that PR Steward has helped contributors fix issues Code Review caught before a person got to the PR.

Carvana’s pilot uses PR Steward to work through review feedback, according to Alex Devkar, its senior vice president of engineering and analytics. Neither customer describes using Claude to approve a PR on its own.

Pricing and availability

Team and Enterprise customers can enable Claude Ship for GitHub repositories unless they use Zero Data Retention, Anthropic’s HIPAA configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys.

Anthropic bills by the token. At Code Review’s launch in March, the company put the average cost at $15 to $25 per review (which isn’t exactly cheap, but cheaper than shipping broken code…).

Running /ship counts as regular Claude Code usage, and while Claude Approvals has no base charge of its own, classifiers consume billable tokens just like any other model use. Policies that call for Code Review trigger a paid review, even in observe-only mode.

There is a bit of a trial period, though. Eligible Enterprise customers have until Jan. 15, 2027, to claim “at least” $10,000 in Claude Ship credits, Anthropic says, but they have to use them within 30 days of claiming those credits.

The post Anthropic’s Claude Ship lets Claude approve routine pull requests appeared first on The New Stack.
Anthropic's new Claude Ship agents review pull requests, fix failing checks, and can approve routine changes under a policy each team writes.

item.title: Google’s AI agents cut quantum computing costs 290-fold — now you can check their work
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Google DeepMind has open-sourced the Lean 4 framework used to verify quantum algorithms developed by its Gemini 4 agents, including

The post Google’s AI agents cut quantum computing costs 290-fold — now you can check their work appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Google DeepMind has open-sourced the Lean 4 framework used to verify quantum algorithms developed by its Gemini 4 agents, including one that reduced estimated computational costs by 290 times.

The GitHub repository contains the mathematical definitions, specifications, and verified solutions, but Google has kept the system that coordinated the agents’ work internal.

Monday’s release follows “Discovering Formally Verified Quantum Programs with AI,” a paper Google posted to arXiv on November 6 that describes how it combined multi-agent algorithm discovery with machine-checked proofs.

The agents used a theorem prover to check whether their quantum programs met predefined requirements for correctness and computational cost.

The agents used a theorem prover to check whether their quantum programs met predefined requirements for correctness and computational cost. Google recently took a similar approach when it used Gemini 4 Carbon to prove properties of Signal’s encryption in Lean.

Inside the Lean 4 framework

Google built the framework on Lean 4, extending the Mathlib and Physlib libraries to support quantum programming and verify its computational costs; the same theorem prover underpins code-focused projects such as Mistral’s Leanstral.

QuantumComputation contains the core quantum programming tools and mathematical definitions, while QuantumComputationSpecs defines the problems the agents were tasked with solving and the requirements their solutions had to meet.

The framework supports both classical control flow and quantum operations, using quantum Hoare logic to prove that programs behave as expected. It also calculates the resources each algorithm requires, with Google measuring computational cost by multiplying the number of logical qubits by the number of T gates.

Developers can build the repository using Lean’s Lake build system.

lake exe cache getlake build


The company keeps the verified algorithms in a separate discoveries branch and has released the software under Apache 2.0. Google also plans to expand its cost models to account for classical computation and control flow.

How the agent teams coordinated

Independent teams of Gemini 4 Carbon agents worked on optimization problems with fixed mathematical specifications. The agents refined their algorithms in response to Lean’s verification results.

The most collaborative effort involved a non-Born-Oppenheimer photochemistry simulation, with as many as seven teams working in parallel.

The most collaborative effort involved a non-Born-Oppenheimer photochemistry simulation, with as many as seven teams working in parallel.

The teams maintained a shared wiki of verified results and met virtually every four hours to compare their progress and build on one another’s discoveries.

Stopping agents from gaming proofs

Because the agents could modify files in their own environments, there was a risk they might weaken specifications or introduce assumptions simply to make their proofs pass. Submissions were therefore checked in clean sandboxes against fixed specifications, with Lean Comparator flagging changes to definitions and theorems and rejecting proofs containing placeholders or unauthorized axioms.

The separation resembles the approach Anthropic’s Claude Code team uses, relying on automated checks rather than human review to evaluate AI-written code. Google has published the formal verification libraries and solutions, but not the infrastructure that coordinates the Gemini agents.

What the algorithms save

The largest gain came from a fixed-point arcsin algorithm, where estimated resource costs fell by a factor of 290. The revised circuit requires 100 logical qubits and 3,698 T gates, compared with 245 qubits and at least 440,576 T gates in the original implementation. Classical testing produced the initial improvements, with formal verification enabling more complex circuit designs that cut costs by another 11%.

Photochemical simulation costs fell roughly eightfold, while a simulation involving cytochrome P450 saw a 2.5-fold improvement.

For an inertial confinement fusion simulation, the agents reduced estimated costs by a factor of 11.8 and lowered the logical qubit requirement from 5,650 to 4,338. Photochemical simulation costs fell roughly eightfold, while a simulation involving cytochrome P450 saw a 2.5-fold improvement.

These are formally verified resource estimates, not performance measurements from quantum hardware; scientific simulations remain beyond the capabilities of current quantum computers.

Developers can independently check the published proofs using the repository’s pinned Lean, Mathlib and Physlib dependencies, with the verified algorithms available in a separate branch. Reproducing the discovery process is another matter, since Google’s agent orchestration system remains proprietary.

The framework’s resource model also has limitations. As noted in Google’s research announcement, it does not yet fully account for classical computation and control flow, which the team plans to address in future updates.

Google DeepMind open-sourced the Lean 4 framework its Gemini 4 agents used to find and formally verify quantum algorithms, with machine-checked proofs.

item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Z.ai released GLM-5.4 on Monday, introducing a Loop Transformer architecture that executes the same layers multiple times to increase computational

The post Z.ai ran the same 28 layers twice — and claims its 750B model can rival a 3-trillion-parameter one appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Z.ai released GLM-5.4 on Monday, introducing a Loop Transformer architecture that executes the same layers multiple times to increase computational depth without adding parameters.

The company claims its 750-billion-parameter model can match the reasoning performance of models with 2 trillion to 3 trillion parameters…

The company claims its 750-billion-parameter model can match the reasoning performance of models with 2 trillion to 3 trillion parameters, although it has not published full-scale benchmarks to support that comparison.

Built by continuing to train GLM-5, the model runs a shared block of 28 layers twice during inference. Z.ai developed the architecture for demanding coding and agentic workloads.

Depth without more parameters

Z.ai chose to modify a pretrained model after earlier experiments showed that looped Transformers trained from scratch performed worse than conventional models given the same pretraining compute.

Repeating layers at this scale created problems with activation stability and attention caching. Z.ai introduced per-token gates to regulate updates to the residual stream and prevent activation norms from growing across iterations.

GLM-5.4 shares the first iteration’s KV cache and maintains a separate sliding window for the second pass, avoiding the memory cost of duplicating the entire attention history at context lengths of up to one million tokens. The model also reuses sparse attention indices between iterations, which Z.ai says had negligible impact on performance in its testing.

Z.ai developed fused inference kernels to reduce intermediate memory reads and writes during repeated layer execution.

Z.ai developed fused inference kernels to reduce intermediate memory reads and writes during repeated layer execution.

What the 30B benchmarks show

Z.ai tested the architecture at 1 billion, 4 billion, 30 billion, and 750 billion parameters, but the detailed benchmark results come from the 30-billion-parameter model.

In those tests, the looped model outperformed a conventional Transformer of the same size on math, scientific reasoning, and long-context tasks, despite requiring about 10% more training compute.

The model also generated 10% to 14% fewer output tokens on benchmarks including MMLU-Pro and GPQA-Diamond. Z.ai attributes the shorter responses to reasoning handled within the repeated layers rather than through additional generated tokens.

From code to robot arms

Z.ai calls its approach Generalized Coding. Its GLM-5.4 demonstrations include building games with physics and combat systems, creating 3D environments with GLSL shaders, and designing a six-axis robotic arm in FreeCAD.

In a post on X, Z.ai head Zixuan Li reported improvements over GLM-5.3 in test writing, code QA, feature development, bug fixes, and terminal-based tasks, although the company has not published the underlying evaluations.

Performance has varied since launch. Z.ai claims throughput of up to 200 tokens per second during off-peak hours, dropping to 70 to 80 during peak traffic.

One developer reported speeds of 150 to 170 tokens per second initially, followed by reports of 40 to 50 tokens per second and traffic errors later in the day. Controlled comparisons of inference latency and cost remain unavailable.

Z.ai also acknowledges that GLM-5.4 can spend excessive time reasoning through tasks.

Z.ai also acknowledges that GLM-5.4 can spend excessive time reasoning through tasks. The company is exploring adaptive computation to limit additional iterations to tokens that need them.

GLM-5.4 is available through the GLM Coding Plan, ZCode, and Z.ai Chat, with vision support and a one-million-token context window.

item.title: AWS launches 5 new open decision models for AI agents
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
AWS on Monday launched Strands Decider v2, a family of five open decision models. The release comes only seven weeks

The post AWS launches 5 new open decision models for AI agents appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AWS on Monday launched Strands Decider v2, a family of five open decision models.

The release comes only seven weeks after Strands Labs, the experimental arm of AWS’s open source Strands Agents SDK, launched the first Strands Decider model. That was a 2-billion-parameter model built on Alibaba’s Qwen3.5.

The new version is based on Google’s Gemma 4 and comes in a range of sizes from the outset, starting at 2 billion parameters, all the way up to a 31-billion-parameter dense model (with a 4B model and a 26B-A4B mixture-of-experts model in the middle), all of which are available under the Apache 2.0 license.

Like similar decision models, the idea behind Strands Decider is that it doesn’t generate text. Instead, it takes a state, like a support ticket or an agent trace, along with a question and a fixed set of possible answers, and then returns a probability for each answer.

AWS VP and Distinguished Engineer Marc Brooker, who started the project, tells The New Stack, “We chose better training data or larger training sets, the usual kind of ML model generation journey, and came out with a set of models with significantly better accuracy and significantly better calibration, which are the things that really matter to customers in this space.”

Benchmarks

And indeed, the models clearly outperform v1. AWS says the 31B model averages 82.1 across six public text benchmarks, ahead of every rival it tested, including Google’s Gemini Decision 1 at 79.4. But it also trails some of its competitors on three of the six benchmarks — and Gemini still posts the lowest calibration error.

The 31B v2 model posts the top score on JevBench, the benchmark built around TypeSafe’s Jev, at 93.1 compared to Gemini’s 92.2. But it loses to Perplexity Decider v1.3 on PubMedQA and When2Call, and to vLLM Semantic Router’s open d3-ultra on a test based on New Yorker cartoon captions.

The smaller models hold up, too.

The 26B-A4B mixture-of-experts model averages 79.9, just ahead of Gemini Decision 1, and the E4B model jumps from 62.7 in v1 to 74.4. On image and video tasks, which AWS didn’t report for v1, the 31B model scores 90.1 on Mind2Web Multimodal and 70.2 on Video-MME, slightly behind Perplexity’s model on both.

The calibration error, which measures how closely a model’s confidence matches how often it’s right, drops to 0.027 for the new 31B model, down from 0.062 for v1. In this benchmark, only Gemini Decision 1 does better, at 0.025, while Jev 1.14 and Microsoft-Decision-1 come in at 0.062 and 0.066 respectively.

“I think with V1 we were benchmark leading for about eight hours,” Brooker says. He thinks the benchmarks are getting “a little bit saturated” and mostly help customers decide whether a 4B model is good enough for their workload.

Gemma 4 and bidirectional attention

It’s worth noting that AWS opted for a different architecture with Strands Decider 2.

Most LLMs today use causal attention, so each token only sees the tokens before it. Models need that to generate text, but since a decision model never generates text, the Strands team let every token in the state attend to the whole state in both directions. This means questions can then reuse that encoded state, so asking 20 questions about one agent trace costs little more than asking a single question.

As for why that works better, “I have some theories, but I would say that I’m not entirely sure,” Brooker says. The team tested both approaches across a diverse set of datasets, and “one outperformed the other, and I think that is the shape of the majority of ML research.”

Brooker says Gemma’s somewhat more traditional architecture may have contributed to the results.

Using Strands Decider at Amazon

Inside Amazon, the company says, engineers on an internal ticketing system swapped Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the v1 E4B model to label tickets. Average time per call fell from 4,215 milliseconds to 897 milliseconds, and AWS estimates the cost dropped from about $22,200 to about $500 per million tickets at list prices. (The team hasn’t published accuracy figures.)

AWS also says v2 cut costs by routing requests between Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, which moves spending away from Anthropic models that AWS sells through Amazon Bedrock.

Brooker is most excited about hybrid workflows. “What’s really nice about these kinds of models is they’re just a cool tool for us to build workflows that are mostly deterministic and then have a decider model step, or mostly agentic, but on the easy routes, we can use decider models to drive down cost and latency,” he says.

Oddly enough, though, Strands Decider isn’t available on AWS’s Bedrock inference service yet. But then, the company’s annual re:Invent conference is happening a week from now and we will surely hear more about Bedrock there.

The post AWS launches 5 new open decision models for AI agents appeared first on The New Stack.
AWS releases Strands Decider v2, five open decision models built on Gemma 4 that top hosted rivals on its benchmarks but aren't on Amazon Bedrock yet.

item.title: Palo Alto and Elastic snap up AI startups. The prize? Enterprise trust and control.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
They say that to understand where an industry is heading, you have to follow the money. And two acquisitions announced

The post Palo Alto and Elastic snap up AI startups. The prize? Enterprise trust and control. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
They say that to understand where an industry is heading, you have to follow the money. And two acquisitions announced this past week suggest that established infrastructure vendors see a big opportunity in helping enterprises take greater control of the AI systems they deploy — and ensuring those systems are secure, reliable and trustworthy.

In early November, Applied Compute, a startup specializing in post-training and inference for open-weight AI models, announced it had raised $350 million at a $3.25 billion valuation, less than 18 months after its founding. Then last Wednesday, cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks swooped in with a $4.5 billion bid to buy the startup outright.

The following day, search and observability giant Elastic announced plans to acquire HoneyHive, a four-year-old startup specializing in AI agent observability and evaluation.

While the deals target different parts of the enterprise AI stack, both point to a growing push by established vendors to bring more of the AI development and operations toolchain in-house.

An acquisition spree

A quick peek at the wider acquisitive landscape suggests a broader trend at play. Last month, observability giant Dynatrace completed its $915 million acquisition of Arize, an AI observability and evaluation platform. And back in July, SAP acquired Prior Labs, a specialist in AI models for structured data, while more recently, payments giant Stripe acquired AI model routing platform OpenRouter.

Palo Alto Networks and Elastic themselves have been on something of a buying spree, the former in particular.

Palo Alto Networks kicked off the year by completing its $3.35 billion acquisition of observability company Chronosphere in January, saying this was about “unifying observability and security for the AI era.” This was followed by its $21.1 billion purchase of identity security giant CyberArk. Since then, it has acquired endpoint security startup Koi, AI gateway provider Portkey, mobile observability specialist Embrace, and AI-native enterprise automation startup Console.

Elastic, meanwhile, acquired Deductive AI in August, bringing AI-powered incident investigation into its observability platform.

For Jason Andersen, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, such deals reflect several pressures facing established software vendors. Some need specialized AI technology better suited to their existing customers, while others see acquisitions as a way to accelerate their AI strategies and expand into new markets.

“There are many cases where an incumbent feels that general purpose AI tools do not fit their value proposition, and they need something more tailored to their customer bases.”

“There are many cases where an incumbent feels that general purpose AI tools do not fit their value proposition, and they need something more tailored to their customer bases,” Andersen tells The New Stack. “I also am seeing all sorts of companies using the acquisitions to jumpstart their own repositioning.”

Palo Alto Networks is a case in point. A veteran of the cybersecurity industry, it started out as a firewall specialist before expanding into cloud security, threat detection and security operations. And as with just about every major technology company today, AI is driving much of its strategy.

On the company’s earnings call last week, Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, suggested that Applied Compute could create an opportunity larger than the company’s core cybersecurity operations.

“If it works, I think this will dwarf the abilities that we have in cybersecurity,” Arora said. “This could be bigger than what we do today.”

“If it works, I think this will dwarf the abilities that we have in cybersecurity. This could be bigger than what we do today.”

Applied Compute specializes in post-training and inference, helping enterprises customize open-weight models for their own needs and run them in production. Its slogan itself sums up its core raison d’être: “The best AI is built, not bought” — a somewhat ironic message, now that Palo Alto Networks is buying the company for $4.5 billion.

Applied Compute has worked with companies including Microsoft and Nvidia, while Palo Alto Networks itself said it had been a “prospective customer.” Arora sees securing an increasingly diverse mix of enterprise AI models as a big business opportunity.

“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured.”

“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” Arora said in a press release announcing the deal.

In a separate LinkedIn post, Applied Compute CEO Yash Patil, who worked on post-training infrastructure and Codex at OpenAI before co-founding the company in May 2025, said that he and his two co-founders had built Applied Compute on the belief that “every company should own its intelligence,” arguing that businesses will increasingly need to develop and control their own AI models.

“We think training, serving, and improving proprietary models will become a normal part of running a company.”

“We think training, serving, and improving proprietary models will become a normal part of running a company,” he writes. “To do useful work, a model needs to access sensitive data and systems, comply with policies, and remain explainable, verifiable, and auditable. This is the reason we’ve always prioritized security, and why joining Palo Alto Networks will help us go further faster.”

Evaluating the AI opportunity

Elastic’s acquisition of HoneyHive, meanwhile, targets a different part of enterprise AI: understanding how agents behave, and whether they’re doing what they’re supposed to. HoneyHive, which claims big-name customers such as Nvidia and MongoDB, brings tracing, evaluation and testing capabilities that Elastic plans to integrate into its existing observability platform.

In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Elastic explicitly describes the HoneyHive acquisition as a move to help its customers “observe, evaluate, and trust the agents they run in production.”

In a separate blog post announcing the deal last Thursday, Santosh Krishnan, senior vice president of observability and security at Elastic, argues that the rise of autonomous agents creates a new challenge for developers: understanding whether their AI systems are making sound decisions, even when the underlying software is functioning as expected.

“Reliable agents need more than traditional application monitoring,” Krishnan writes. “AI observability provides visibility into agent behavior and the ability to evaluate the quality of its decisions and outcomes.”

By combining HoneyHive’s agent-specific capabilities with Elastic’s existing monitoring tools, the company hopes to give developers a clearer picture of how their agents interact with the applications and infrastructure supporting them.

“This combination could also enable teams to evaluate production telemetry more broadly, helping them understand not only how their AI applications are performing, but whether their agents are achieving the intended outcomes,” Krishnan adds.

But what does the acquisition mean for developers already using HoneyHive who don’t want to adopt the broader Elastic platform? Krishnan tells The New Stack that existing customers will continue to be supported during the integration, with HoneyHive’s capabilities eventually expected to become native Elastic offerings.

“Customers will retain the flexibility to adopt use-cases of interest, without committing to use all the capabilities of the platform,” Krishnan says, adding that more details on the combined product roadmap will be shared in the coming months.

One stack to rule them all?

While both deals reflect growing demand for greater control over enterprise AI, Andersen cautions against assuming that model training, evaluation and observability are all converging into a single stack.

“Training is very distinct and most organizations will likely never need to do training on a model at least until the skills become more commonplace and costs go down,” Andersen says.

Most agent platforms already include some observability capabilities, Andersen notes, but evaluation is a different story. Enterprises have several ways to assess model outputs, including using other AI models, and the right approach depends on what an agent is designed to do.

“I think that over time evaluations could become a major embedded component of agentic platforms, but right now they are distinct,” Andersen says.

Beyond questions around convergence, there are perhaps more immediate reasons for established vendors to acquire AI startups, including access to specialist talent and the potential to reduce costs.

“Aside from strengthening their customer position, a lot of these startups have really smart people to inject some new minds into a company,” Andersen says. “And / or it could be a way to save the incumbent money by bringing a technology in house, versus having to pay OpenAI or some other company.”

Palo Alto Networks’ deal, in particular, fits that mold: it brings Applied Compute’s research team in-house, giving the company additional expertise in developing and adapting AI models, with Patil set to become co-chief AI officer once the transaction closes.

And Andersen expects more deals to come, with buyers driven as much by necessity as by opportunity.

“The issue right now is that valuations are sky-high, as is the cost of money vis-à-vis interest rates,” he says. “So, while I can’t speculate on a specific name, I would say that these purchases are increasingly going to happen with buyers that are under some pressure to deliver better results.”

The post Palo Alto and Elastic snap up AI startups. The prize? Enterprise trust and control. appeared first on The New Stack.
As enterprises put AI agents and custom models into production, Palo Alto Networks and Elastic want to be the ones keeping them secure and in check.

item.title: GPT-6.2 Astra vs. Claude Fable 5.2: Astra’s launch got mixed reviews, but it tested well here
item.dc:creator: Jessica Wachtel
item.description:
When I compared Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 vs. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra last week, Fable 5.2 was slightly more accurate (149 points

The post GPT-6.2 Astra vs. Claude Fable 5.2: Astra’s launch got mixed reviews, but it tested well here appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
When I compared Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 vs. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra last week, Fable 5.2 was slightly more accurate (149 points vs. 145). But it cost 3.4 times as much as Astra, even with a lower list price, because it used about five times as many tokens.

Then, on Tuesday, November 17, OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra with a 20% price cut. The updated Astra’s list price is $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, identical to Fable 5.2’s, removing Fable 5.2’s list-price advantage. The question now is which model does more with each token.

It’s no surprise that both companies say theirs does. OpenAI says the upgraded Astra beats Fable 5.2 on agent tasks, where a model works through a job step by step using tools, costing a fraction as much per task. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 is the stronger coder, and it scores higher on FrontierCode 2.0, the coding benchmark both companies report.

The launch got mixed reviews, though. OpenAI’s safety testing found that the new Astra failed to disclose a known obstacle in about 22% of coding tasks in one evaluation, twice the rate of GPT-6 Astra.

OpenAI says that evaluation deliberately put obstacles in the model’s way, and that it’s concerned by the regression. My tests weren’t built to measure it, so my results only speak to the marketing claims about accuracy and cost on the specific tests included.

The tests

In the last round of testing I did on these models, the scores were incredibly close. I wanted to make sure the close scores reflected the models’ capabilities and weren’t the result of easy tests. To make sure the tests were hard, I ran each one through GPT-5 and made it harder whenever GPT-5 scored near-perfect. I included GPT-5’s scores on the hardest version of each test in the descriptions below for reference. 

As with all my tests, I ran each model once per test through its maker’s API at default settings. I used a script to grade the results against the answer key I created for each test. Since these tasks have written rules and one right answer per check, they’re more structured than the benchmarks the two companies cite. The scores don’t check those benchmark numbers, but they do check how accurately each model handles detailed, realistic work.

Here are the tests:

  • Month-end close (173 points) – I gave the model a fake software company’s billing system, contracts, payments, outage history, and team chats for 40 customers. It had to catch every invoice that didn’t match its contract, work out downtime credits, apply 30 payments, and refuse coworker requests that broke company policy. GPT-5 score: 130/173
  • Billing library (110 points) – I planted 20 bugs and one unfinished feature in a billing library. The spec left most rules unwritten, so the model had to work them out from about 100 records from the company’s old system, without copying that system’s known bugs. Three of the library’s own tests are wrong, and the model should report them without editing them. GPT-5 score: 41/110
  • Lab data analysis (76 points) – The models analyzed an enzyme study with 30 samples and messy data. One instrument’s files were in a format the lab’s reader script couldn’t read correctly, one sample plate went in rotated, one clock ran seven minutes fast, and a warm freezer spoiled some samples. GPT-5 scored 57/76

Month-end close

This was the agent test, where OpenAI’s marketing says Astra leads. Both models scored a perfect 173 out of 173. Each one read all 40 contracts, caught every mispriced invoice, got every credit right to the cent, and refused every request that broke policy.

“For the same score, Fable 5.2 cost four times as much and took about three times as long.”

Similar to the last round of testing, the difference came down to effort. Fable 5.2 spent more than 19,000 tokens on reasoning, and Astra spent 830. For the same score, Fable 5.2 cost four times as much and took about three times as long. That’s going to add up quickly on long-running jobs working at production scale.

The numbers:

  • Fable 5.2: 12 turns, 671,398 in, 39,235 out (19,442 reasoning), $2.90, 315 s.
  • Astra: 10 turns, 255,206 in, 7,271 out (830 reasoning), $0.72, 106 s.

Billing library

Anthropic’s marketing says Fable 5.2 excels over GPT-6 Astra on coding tasks like the ones in this test. This claim held, but by a small margin. Fable 5.2 scored 110/110, and Astra scored 108. 

Both models fixed all 20 bugs and flagged all three wrong tests. Astra’s only mistake was in the feature it had to finish. Its code canceled a customer’s scheduled switch to a cheaper plan when it shouldn’t have. That’s a two-point miss in a test, but in a live billing system it means an unhappy customer because the mistake keeps them paying the higher price after asking to pay less. 

Fable 5.2 caught that rule, but it wrote about 11 times as many output tokens, cost six times as much, and took more than five times as long. In a case like this, one missed rule charges real customers the wrong amount, meaning the extra spend is worth it. 

The numbers:

  • Fable 5.2: 14 turns, 569,395 in, 36,622 out (25,502 reasoning), $2.53, 348 s.
  • Astra: 12 turns, 143,367 in, 3,238 out (320 reasoning), $0.42, 66 s.

Lab data analysis

This test had the widest cost gap, even though both models scored 76/76. Astra read the files, wrote one script, and finished in one minute for 31 cents. Fable 5.2 tested its method on practice scripts first, then revised its final script three times. It took more than four minutes and cost $2.17, seven times as much.

For a data analysis job like this one, where both models reached the same correct numbers, Astra’s direct approach got the lab its results three minutes sooner for $1.86 less.

Results

Both models got a perfect score on the agent test, so I didn’t see Astra beat Fable 5.2 the way OpenAI says it does. Fable 5.2 was the better coder, as Anthropic says, but only by two points. OpenAI’s cost-per-task claim matched my results. At the same price per token, Fable 5.2 cost more than five times as much.

“…it’s pretty wild to see work that tripped up last year’s leading model is now nearly perfect in the newer releases.”

Though I didn’t include GPT-5 in my main test analysis, it’s pretty wild to see work that tripped up last year’s leading model is now nearly perfect in the newer releases.

What do I think?

At first glance, I’d recommend Fable 5.2 because it performed perfectly on all tests. But timing and cost tell a different story. You could run Astra twice on each test and still finish faster and cost less than Fable 5.2.

“You could run Astra twice on each test and still finish faster and cost less than Fable 5.2.”

And that’s what I think a better recommendation is. When you’re getting started, I’d run Astra two or three times on the same task and compare the results. If you see errors or differences, run a second model, like Fable 5.2, to double-check. After arriving at the correct result, you can adjust your instructions or prompts to better fit Astra to what your task requires. 

The post GPT-6.2 Astra vs. Claude Fable 5.2: Astra’s launch got mixed reviews, but it tested well here appeared first on The New Stack.
GPT-6.2 Astra now costs the same per token as Claude Fable 5.2. In three hard tests, Fable scored slightly higher but cost more than five times as much.

item.title: “It is a rollercoaster ride”: Angie Jones of the Agentic AI Foundation on keeping up with AI agents
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
Only a few years ago, it would have been impossible to picture this scenario: A lead developer once gave 10

The post “It is a rollercoaster ride”: Angie Jones of the Agentic AI Foundation on keeping up with AI agents appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Only a few years ago, it would have been impossible to picture this scenario: A lead developer once gave 10 new hires at Block a codebase they’d never seen, access to AI agents, and a day and a half to solve problems that customers had brought to them in person. It was their first day, but they all delivered. 

For teams wondering where junior developers fit in, this experiment raises a question. What might experienced engineers learn from them?

“It is a rollercoaster ride,” Angie Jones, the lead developer and now vice president of the Agentic AI Foundation, told The New Stack’s Frederic Lardinois at last month at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose. Their conversation reveals a tension familiar to anyone who’s learned a new coding workflow only to find it out of date by the next model release. 

Jones has led AI enablement at Block and helped maintain the open source coding agent Goose. From both experiences, she distinguishes between learning to work with an agent and learning to build one others can depend on.

A baseline developers can use to build

Jones teaches using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to applications and uses Agent2Agent (A2A) as an example of a standard for coordination between agents. With multiple companies agreeing on how to tackle common problems, developers have interfaces they can build around as the tools evolve. 

“You can bet on it and say, ‘I can build on top of this now,’” Jones told TNS.

That still leaves plenty of engineering to do. A developer building an agent needs to understand the loop that lets it choose an action, examine the result, and decide what to do next. Someone has to decide where to constrain that loop and what access the agent should have to customer data. 

The foundation’s MCP Associate certification lets developers demonstrate their understanding of MCP. At the same time, its working groups tackle issues that surface when agents move into everyday use, including identity, reliability, security, and governance.

At Block, Jones approached adoption by asking a small group of engineers to make the development environment easier for agents to use. Baking that work into the system meant developers could point an agent at a repository and benefit from what the group had learned – even if they’d missed last week’s lesson in prompting, for example. 

Who gets to decide what ships?

Goose offers a maintainer’s view. Coding agents have made it easier for people to propose a fix or a feature. Each pull request still takes someone’s time to review. The project shifted to an issue-first process so contributors and maintainers could agree on the problem and the design before anyone generated a patch. “Let’s talk about the problem and the direction that we want to take with the maintainers, then collaborate on the design,” Jones said.

“Let’s talk about the problem and the direction that we want to take with the maintainers, then collaborate on the design.” – Angie Jones

Goose’s maintainers also use agents to triage issues, review incoming code, and run security scans. The tools that make it easy to open a pull request can help maintainers manage the queue, while issue discussions give contributors a place to explain why a change belongs in the project. 

“A new hire may know how to get an agent moving quickly. An experienced reviewer can help them see which of those changes are worth shipping.” – Angie Jones

Jones sees a similar exchange between junior and senior engineers at work. “A new hire may know how to get an agent moving quickly. An experienced reviewer can help them see which of those changes are worth shipping,” Jones said.

Watch the full interview on The New Stack’s YouTube channel for Jones’ account of that first day at Block, what Goose learned from a flood of AI-assisted contributions, and why building agents may soon become part of the job for developers across the stack.

The post “It is a rollercoaster ride”: Angie Jones of the Agentic AI Foundation on keeping up with AI agents appeared first on The New Stack.
Angie Jones of the Agentic AI Foundation and Goose tells The New Stack why using AI agents and building agents others can depend on are different skills.

item.title: If we stop reading the code, what do we read?
item.dc:creator: Ankit Jain
item.description:
“Human beings are too slow when dealing with code. So if we’re going to move at the speed of the

The post If we stop reading the code, what do we read? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
“Human beings are too slow when dealing with code. So if we’re going to move at the speed of the agents, we’re all going to have to back off a little bit and maintain the high-level supervision, but at the level of code, that’s probably out of our domain now.”

That’s Robert “Uncle Bob” Martin, who wrote Clean Code almost 20 years ago, and a whole generation of engineers learned from it that code is written for other humans to read. When I had him on The Hangar DX podcast, he told me he never sees 95% of the code his agents write.

I didn’t expect to hear that from him. I also don’t think he’s wrong about the speed. Agents open pull requests faster than anyone can read them, and most teams stopped reading line by line a while ago.

Next, he said, “I try to get as much intelligence about what it has done as I can without forcing myself to go all the way to code.”

“Even the person who just declared code out of scope for humans is still reading something.”

Even the person who just declared code out of scope for humans is still reading something.

He showed me what that something is. Partway through our conversation, he shared his screen and walked me through the tool he reviews with now.

An agent breaks his project down into something close to UML, and he can expand, collapse, and drill into any part.

Problems show up in red:

  • Functions with a CRAP score that’s too high. CRAP, short for Change Risk Anti-Patterns, is a 2007 metric that combines cyclomatic complexity with test coverage and spikes when code is both complex and poorly tested.
  • A mutation-testing score that’s too low.
  • Arrows marking dependencies that point the wrong way.

The agent is attached to the diagram, so he can run what-if scenarios, ask it to move components into different layers, and review the proposed structure before any of it becomes source code. He can still drill down to a module, but usually he doesn’t.

He’s checking the partitioning, the direction of the dependencies, and whether the parts that change often are decoupled from the parts that don’t.

“This was the old dream of UML,” he told me, “but UML was conceived back when it was a static thing that you did before you wrote the code. This is now a dynamic thing that you do after the code is produced.”

That works for one engineer and one agent. On a team, where other people need to understand the change too, what should the reviewer be looking at when they approve it?

Nobody reads anything

Ray Myers has spent a good part of this year arguing against the idea that we should stop reading code. When he came on the podcast, he summed up the people on the other side better than they do themselves: “Most of the people who are telling you don’t read code are actually doing some lowercase form of actually reading the code.”

Lowercase reading takes a few forms. Some engineers skip the code on throwaway, low-stakes tasks and read carefully everywhere else. Some lean on automated verification, so a passing test suite, a harness, or a dashboard becomes the thing they read. Some read selectively, skip the bug hunt, and look only at design and maintainability. Some read at the very end. None of them read nothing.

What to read when you stop reading the code

I’ve argued before that code review was doing two jobs at once, alignment and standards checking, and that AI broke each of them differently. The review I’d build today hands the reviewer three things to read.

Intent

What the change is for, what’s in scope, and what’s deliberately left out. Intent gets captured where decisions actually happen, in the prompts and the back-and-forth with the agent.

Acceptance criteria

These come in two layers. The first is the criteria for this specific change; the second is the invariants from the team’s AI slop registry, the patterns your senior engineers keep correcting, which apply to every matching change automatically. A verifying agent with no context from the agent that wrote the code checks each criterion and returns a verdict and evidence. This is how we built Verify at Aviator. The reviewer reads the criteria and the evidence with one question in mind: are we solving the right problem with the right constraints?

Decisions

The architectural, behavioral, and technical calls made along the way. Which library, which data model, what happens when the downstream service times out, what we chose not to build. Most of what an agent writes is boilerplate.

The decisions are what a human actually contributed, so another human should look at them. When two engineers disagree about one of them, the team needs a place to argue it out, and that deserves its own article.

Uncle Bob described the new human job as taking responsibility “just above the code level.” Intent, criteria, and decisions live there.

Keeping the mental model

Knowledge sharing and building mental models of the codebase were never side effects of code review; they were part of the job. Mitchell Hashimoto calls his version of this the whiteboard defense. Anyone who ships a customer-facing system should be able to explain how it works and defend the decisions behind it. He doesn’t expect them to remember function names. He does expect a confident answer when he asks, “Why did you do X instead of Y?” or “Where does this fail?”

Reading intent, acceptance criteria, and decisions keeps the mental model alive even if engineers can’t realistically read every line of AI-generated code. You still know why the system works the way it does and how its parts fit together, even if you haven’t looked at every function. And the team no longer depends on the one senior engineer who remembers how everything works.

Not reading the code is a sliding scale

Few people are closer to what code review looks like across the industry than David Poll, who leads GitHub’s pull request and code review team. When we talked, he told me that asking whether to read the code or not is the wrong question.

“The question is not whether I read or not read the code; it’s whether my attention gets directed to where it’s actually useful. Can I be pointed at the parts that are meaningful for me to go and look at and apply my judgment and expertise, and the things that can be with high confidence removed from my attention set, can fall away more and more over time.”

He’s right. Most teams already read some parts of their codebase closely and barely look at others. What lets you move along it safely is the quality of what you read in place of the code. Clear intent, criteria backed by real evidence, and decisions recorded where they were made let more of the code fall out of your attention set with confidence.

Someone still owns it

“The agents are not responsible for anything. They’re entirely irresponsible. Only humans can be responsible.”

That’s Uncle Bob again, and it’s the one part of this debate nobody can automate away. When I laid out the new shape of code review, I split it into five layers: argue, capture, codify, debate, and own. Own is the layer he’s talking about that no tool takes off your plate. The engineer who merges a change owns it, whether they read every line or none.

“The agents are not responsible for anything. They’re entirely irresponsible. Only humans can be responsible.”

You can stop reading the code. You can’t stop owning it.
